problem: Standard RL with elementary actions cannot solve navigation in large, multi-room scenes with sparse rewards, since random exploration is practically infeasible. Prior topological-map navigation is simpler and not trained by RL.
motivation: Injecting external world knowledge about space (objects, topological connectivity) into the action design can offload exploration from the RL algorithm. Topological maps are efficient planning tools and biologically plausible.
key_idea: Build an object-oriented topological map whose nodes are detected objects and use them as macro actions (go to object) for a DQN, with a shortest-path planner translating macro actions into elementary moves.
insight: Object-based macro actions plus an explored-flag exploration bonus let a simple DQN solve sequential multi-object search under purely sparse rewards, where elementary-action RL is practically impossible. Evidence is only training curves showing decreasing episode length (steps per episode) for 1, 2 and 3 targets, with both intermediate and final-only rewards; no baselines or ablations are reported.
method: Object-oriented topological map: whenever an object is detected in an RGBD frame, its position is estimated from agent pose, viewing angle and depth, and a node is created storing the object's bounding-box pixels, position and an explored flag.
Edges and explored flags: an edge is added when the agent moves from one node to another; a node is marked explored when the agent has been close to it.
Macro actions: each map-stored object is an action (navigate to it), translated into elementary actions via graph shortest-path; the action space grows with the map.
Modified DQN: a CNN takes the outer product of one action's feature (object pixels) and a one-hot task-progress state vector, inspired by He et al. 2016 (DRRN-style), to output a Q-value per action.
Action selection: Q-values are computed iteratively for all map objects and the argmax is chosen; unexplored nodes receive a Q-value bonus to encourage exploration.
Assumed perception: SLAM and object detection are assumed to work; ground truth from Habitat is used instead.

setting.backbone: DQN with a CNN (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: RL trained in Habitat 2.0 with HM3D, 100 scenes with varying goal positions per scene; sparse rewards (+1 per subgoal or +1 only at the end)
setting.observation: RGB-D with ground-truth object detection and pose (SLAM assumed)
setting.action_space: Object-level macro actions (go to a map node), executed via graph shortest path; limit of 250 macro actions per episode
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object detection/recognition and localization used in place of SLAM and detector

numbers_note: Results are given only as training curves in a figure (steps per episode); no numeric table.
results: Episode length in macro steps decreases during training for 1, 2 and 3 sequential targets, under both intermediate and final-only rewards, indicating the agent learns to re-recognize objects and learn their order. No quantitative comparison to baselines is reported.
limitations: Long training time and reliance on handcrafted map heuristics
Assumes working SLAM and object detection (ground truth used); only colored cylinder targets tested so far
Only qualitative training curves; no baselines or quantitative metrics (SR/SPL)
